_wxQdcjzlZ4.title: The Potential for Change
_wxQdcjzlZ4.one_line: The London Muslim Survey and Gaza show a community with every tool it needs for change. What is missing is the belief that each person carries weight.
_wxQdcjzlZ4.summary: He reads the much-quoted ayah on Allah not changing a people's condition until they change themselves as a warning that change works in both directions. He then summarizes the Social Innovation Lab's London Muslim Survey. The community has high potential: it is young, educated, skilled and wealthy. But immigrants struggle once their savings run out, many people feel isolated and do not belong, masjids are not equipped to help, and courage and wisdom rarely appear together. He also notes the alarming number of Muslims leaving Canada, the stigma around mental health, and a habit of describing problems instead of trying solutions. He turns to Gaza: powers now kill openly without even pretending to an ethical justification, and those killed are not like us, they are us. His conclusion is careful: he will not say change will happen, only that it can, because the community lacks none of the tools, only the willpower. The second khutbah uses the hadith of the hundred camels, the conversions of Hamza and Umar, and Umar's four men each worth a thousand to argue that one committed person can carry great weight. He asks people to carry this belief into Ramadan as their intention.

outline.heading: Opening
The most overused ayah
outline.gist: The verse on change is quoted so often it loses its meaning, yet it holds a law Allah set in His Book for us to live by.

outline.heading: Interlude
A threat more than a law
outline.gist: Summarizing the Social Innovation Lab's London Muslim Survey, he reads Allah's promise not to change a people's state until they change themselves as a warning: if you want things to stay good, do not change for the worse. It works from bad to good as well.

outline.heading: What the survey can tell us
outline.gist: Some six hundred families, mostly from northwest London, so the east and south are underrepresented; still, the data gives real information for next steps.

outline.heading: High potential, weak output
outline.gist: The community is youthful, well educated, skilled and wealthy, so its potential is very high; the problem is connecting people, and the gap between very rich and very poor is huge.

outline.heading: Newcomers struggle once savings run out
outline.gist: Immigrants manage the first year or two, then struggle socially, financially and spiritually from the third year, because the community does not embrace and integrate them.

outline.heading: Isolation, and masjids not equipped to help
outline.gist: Many feel alone when they want to marry, buy a house, find a job or face discrimination, and do not know their rights. They do not feel safe coming to the masjid because they are turned away too often by institutions unprepared to help.

outline.heading: Bystanders in their own community
outline.gist: People come, pray and leave, uninterested in community issues because they feel the community belongs to someone else and they are only visitors.

outline.heading: Courage and wisdom seldom come together
outline.gist: Either people have too much courage and yell without results, or they see what must be done but are afraid, especially parents asking about their children's identity and rights at school; many simply do not know whom to go to.

outline.heading: Muslims leaving Canada
outline.gist: In the last year and a half he has never seen so many Muslims pack up and leave, the reverse of the usual. It is not only the economy: lacking the backbone to speak up is a communal problem.

outline.heading: Mental health: jinn, magic and years untreated
outline.gist: Diagnoses remain taboo; people are told it is a spell or a jinn and passed around for years without professional care until it is hard to help them. A broken leg goes to a doctor, and a broken psyche needs a professional too.

outline.heading: Good at describing problems, afraid to try solutions
outline.gist: We describe deficits well but rarely attempt solutions and have no systematic approach, in masjids or out, because anyone who tries and fails is eaten alive by those who do nothing.

outline.heading: Islam is a social innovation lab
outline.gist: Islam came, looked at all of society's problems and solved them through Allah's guidance; we already have the approaches and solutions and need people willing to carry them as what they owe the ummah.

outline.heading: The old rule: power had to look ethical
outline.gist: In the struggle for power, rulers always had to appear to abide by ethics in public. For the first time in his life he sees that no longer cared about: a veto cast with no explanation at all.

outline.heading: Hospitals, rubble and starvation with no explanation
outline.gist: Bombing hospitals, pulling children from rubble hourly, crowding a population into a small area and starving it, with no attempt at justification even from governments that claim to represent their people.

outline.heading: They are not like us; they are us
outline.gist: The people being killed share our names and backgrounds; there is no difference between Muslims wherever they live.

outline.heading: The sanctity of life is not debatable
outline.gist: Killing one soul unlawfully is like killing humanity and saving one is like saving humanity; keep the verse in mind as we watch what is happening now.

outline.heading: Can, not will: no false hope
outline.gist: He chooses his words carefully: he will not say change is happening or will happen, because he does not sell illusions or wishful thinking.

outline.heading: We lack none of the tools
outline.gist: What is factual is that change can happen. Others in history lacked leadership, guidance, resources, numbers or youth; this community has all of them.

outline.heading: What is missing is the willpower
outline.gist: The missing piece is the belief that you are important in the equation of change. One Muslim in a little-known city of 36,000 can spark a different reality, but only if he believes it.

outline.heading: Change began with a few young believers
outline.gist: Arguing big-picture politics is pointless when no one listens to us; what we can talk about is change from ourselves. The Prophet started with simple individuals like Ali and teenagers who had little reason to think they mattered, and change began in their hearts.

outline.heading: Change starts in the heart, not outside you
outline.gist: It can start in your heart right now, unseen. Attending and then living as before while expecting things to change externally is misguided.

outline.heading: One worth ten, downgraded to two
outline.gist: The ratio of one believer to ten was lowered to one to two because of weakness, but it never actually fell that low in the Prophet's lifetime except at Hunayn, where they nearly lost everything; otherwise it was one to three, four, fifteen and beyond ten.

outline.heading: Interlude
A hundred camels, barely one to ride
outline.gist: In the hadith in Al-Bukhari, people are like a hundred camels among which you can hardly find one dependable. Most Muslims do not even come to Jumuah; if they did, four more masjids this size would be needed.

outline.heading: Are you amongst the few?
outline.gist: Few of My servants are grateful: few internalize their understanding of Allah and live it. Being in the masjid puts you among the few, and if the few have no intention of change, what hope is there?

outline.heading: Weight in the years of persecution
outline.gist: You can carry weight in your community, not physical weight. Read years five to eight of the seerah: the Prophet tortured and defamed, companions laid on hot coals, smoked and killed.

outline.heading: Hamza: a conversion with its own chapter
outline.gist: Amid all those stories, every seerah book stops for the Islam of two men as if it were a cosmic event, because of their weight. Hamza's Islam meant Muslims knew they could go to him for protection.

outline.heading: Umar: prayer at the Kaaba openly
outline.gist: We were humiliated until Umar accepted Islam; then they prayed openly at the Kaaba and no one dared speak. The point is impact, not physical strength.

outline.heading: Four men worth a thousand
outline.gist: Amr ibn al-As, stuck in the conquest of Egypt, asked for 8,000 troops and saw only 4,000 arrive; Umar's letter said each thousand was led by a man worth a thousand. After the conquest Amr wrote back that the four alone would have been enough.

outline.heading: People of weight see the need and go for it
outline.gist: They are not distracted, do not wait for applause or permission, and feel ownership because Islam is their story; then one person is worth a thousand. Or we stay exactly as we are and expect a miracle.

outline.heading: Lands in turmoil in his lifetime
outline.gist: At 38 he lists from memory Kosovo, Kashmir, Pakistan, Myanmar, China, Somalia, Sudan, Libya, Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt, Yemen, Lebanon, Iraq, his own Syria and the Holy Land.

outline.heading: What will you change inside?
outline.gist: If you do not want that to continue, what will you do? Do you feel this ummah is yours, or will you keep listening to complaints, make dua and walk out unchanged? He is tired too, but there is a point.

outline.heading: Can: the intention to take into Ramadan
outline.gist: Can is the only word he can honestly use; anything stronger would be selling wishful thinking. Take that intention into your heart before Ramadan.

outline.heading: Outro

XGEjdid3kWU.title: Ramadan Prep: The Philosophy of Fasting
XGEjdid3kWU.one_line: Why Allah prescribed fasting: taqwa, self-discipline, separating wants from needs, gratitude, empathy, breaking bad habits, and filling the inner emptiness with Allah.
XGEjdid3kWU.summary: Before Ramadan he lays out the philosophy behind fasting. It is the ritual the self resists most and the first to disappear when religions are altered, yet in Islam it remains the year's most cherished month. Its goal is taqwa, which he defines as a simple filter: will this harm me now or later? From there he draws several lessons. Fasting proves you can tell the self no, because only a fasting human refuses food when hungry, and only Allah has the authority to ask it with no one watching; the question is never whether you can but whether you will. It separates what you want from what you need. It resets expectations, so blessings are appreciated and we expect less from Allah and more from ourselves, while hunger should breed empathy for those who fast involuntarily. Ramadan is a large adjustment, ideal for breaking bad habits, so he asks people to list theirs. Good behaviour should come because of fasting, not despite it, just as faith grows because of trials. Using the liver's ability to generate fuel internally, he argues our strength comes from within. Fasting clears distractions so the endless inner emptiness can be filled with Allah alone. Practically, he urges a light iftar and eating less.

outline.heading: The first ritual to disappear
outline.gist: When faiths were altered, fasting was dropped first because it is hardest; even now everyone feels a little worry before Ramadan.

outline.heading: Where the self draws the line
outline.gist: The nafs tolerates many disciplines but rebels at food and drink, yet in Islam fasting survives and Ramadan holds everyone's best memories.

outline.heading: Taqwa as a safety valve
outline.gist: Fasting aims at taqwa, a simple question before any act: will this harm me now or later? It ignores the neutral and simply holds you back from regret.

outline.heading: Self-discipline: who is at the wheel?
outline.gist: We know what helps, have the tools and want it, yet do not do it, because the nafs is steering while letting us think we are; Ramadan returns control.

outline.heading: Proof that you can say no
outline.gist: Any healthy hungry mammal eats; only a fasting human refuses, on the authority of Allah alone with no one watching; the question is not 'can you' but 'will you'.

outline.heading: What you want is not what you need
outline.gist: The nafs always wants more house, car, status and money; wanting is fine, but it is not need.

outline.heading: Be careful with 'I need'
outline.gist: If you can work all day without food or water, the rest of the year you only wanted it; the starving can say 'need', most of us cannot.

outline.heading: The nafs adapts
outline.gist: After two days of caffeine headaches the last day of Ramadan is a walk in the park; the self adapts, we just rarely let it adapt to something better.

outline.heading: Imagining the first Ramadan
outline.gist: Farmers and shepherds under the Arabian noon sun hearing that they must fast every day, every year, and then go to battle while fasting.

outline.heading: Badr in the very first Ramadan
outline.gist: The most important battle in Muslim history came in their first Ramadan with no warm-up, showing Ramadan is a time to be at one's most productive.

outline.heading: 'I'm fasting' is a promise, not a threat
outline.gist: Saying you are fasting means you will not trade insults or let ego win, not that your patience has run out.

outline.heading: The happiest day at work
outline.gist: His first workday after Ramadan, with tea and lunch back, makes him the happiest person in the clinic; fasting makes blessings visible.

outline.heading: Expectations and entitlement
outline.gist: Expect 100 and get 90 and you feel cheated; we resent our children's entitlement but treat Allah the same way, fixating on the one missing piece.

outline.heading: Those who fast involuntarily
outline.gist: Some lack clean water or food; his cancer patients sit before good meals they cannot eat or even smell.

outline.heading: Expect more from yourself
outline.gist: If you managed this much without food and water, you can clearly do more; expect more of yourself instead of more from Allah.

outline.heading: Hunger should breed empathy
outline.gist: The fasting person should be the most empathetic, not the one honking in traffic, and may dedicate a life to being the voice of the hungry.

outline.heading: Do not fast feeling sorry for yourself
outline.gist: You are stronger and more capable than you know; expect less from your surroundings and from Allah and more from yourself.

outline.heading: Good habits need small adjustments
outline.gist: Overeating and reversing day and night defeat the point; good habits come from small steps repeated daily for a long time.

outline.heading: Bad habits need a large adjustment
outline.gist: Addictions are broken cold turkey, not by tapering; Ramadan is exactly that kind of large adjustment.

outline.heading: Ramadan is built to strip bad habits
outline.gist: Done properly it makes a bad habit almost impossible to keep; its intensity is not meant to last all year, since Allah draws hearts in that month, so write down the habits you want gone.

outline.heading: Because of fasting, not despite it
outline.gist: Do not be patient or kind 'despite' fasting; be so because you are fasting, and fix the language that frames it as a burden.

outline.heading: Faith grows because of trials
outline.gist: We believe because of hardship, not despite it; the most tested are the prophets then the most pious, so Ramadan is a mountain of strength, not a weakness.

outline.heading: The idle liver
outline.gist: Constant eating leaves the liver with nothing to do, like idle clerks at desks, until it grows lazy and fatty.

outline.heading: Gluconeogenesis: power from within
outline.gist: When the brain and stomach complain, the liver makes fuel internally for days or weeks; biology itself shows your source of strength is inside you.

outline.heading: Fast like you just accepted Islam
outline.gist: New Muslims describing their first prostration or first fast bring him to tears; approach this Ramadan as new, as the companions did their first.

outline.heading: The black hole inside
outline.gist: Everyone carries an emptiness that swallows food, travel, parties, substances and work and only grows hungrier; only the love and nearness of Allah fills it.

outline.heading: Fasting removes the distractions
outline.gist: If even food and drink are treated as distractions, so is everything else; everyone who finally got their worldly goal found it was not worth it.

outline.heading: Ambition for Allah's pleasure
outline.gist: Stay ambitious, but to please Allah rather than fill the void; one night of weeping in prayer will feel like the most valuable moment of your life, so use food for need, not as a master.

outline.heading: A light iftar, then the masjid
outline.gist: Break the fast with dates, water and a little soup, pray and go to taraweeh, instead of arriving overfull and unable to hear the Quran.

outline.heading: Eat less
outline.gist: Do not pile the day's meals into iftar; break the fast promptly as the sunnah says but eat less, as he has for nearly two decades, and finish the month energised.

outline.heading: Outro

36:13.ar: وَٱضۡرِبۡ لَهُم مَّثَلًا أَصۡحَٰبَ ٱلۡقَرۡيَةِ إِذۡ جَآءَهَا ٱلۡمُرۡسَلُونَ
36:13.en: Coin for them a similitude: The people of the city when those sent (from Allah) came unto them

36:14.ar: إِذۡ أَرۡسَلۡنَآ إِلَيۡهِمُ ٱثۡنَيۡنِ فَكَذَّبُوهُمَا فَعَزَّزۡنَا بِثَالِثࣲ فَقَالُوٓاْ إِنَّآ إِلَيۡكُم مُّرۡسَلُونَ
36:14.en: When We sent unto them twain, and they denied them both, so We reinforced them with a third, and they said: Lo! we have been sent unto you

36:15.ar: قَالُواْ مَآ أَنتُمۡ إِلَّا بَشَرࣱ مِّثۡلُنَا وَمَآ أَنزَلَ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنُ مِن شَيۡءٍ إِنۡ أَنتُمۡ إِلَّا تَكۡذِبُونَ
36:15.en: They said: Ye are but mortals like unto us. The Beneficent hath naught revealed. Ye do but lie

36:16.ar: قَالُواْ رَبُّنَا يَعۡلَمُ إِنَّآ إِلَيۡكُمۡ لَمُرۡسَلُونَ
36:16.en: They answered: Our Lord knoweth that we are indeed sent unto you

36:17.en: And our duty is but plain conveyance (of the message)

36:18.ar: قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّا تَطَيَّرۡنَا بِكُمۡۖ لَئِن لَّمۡ تَنتَهُواْ لَنَرۡجُمَنَّكُمۡ وَلَيَمَسَّنَّكُم مِّنَّا عَذَابٌ أَلِيمࣱ‏
36:18.en: (The people of the city) said: We augur ill of you. If ye desist not, we shall surely stone you, and grievous torture will befall you at our hands

36:19.ar: قَالُواْ طَٰٓئِرُكُم مَّعَكُمۡ أَئِن ذُكِّرۡتُمۚ بَلۡ أَنتُمۡ قَوۡمࣱ مُّسۡرِفُونَ
36:19.en: They said: Your evil augury be with you! Is it because ye are reminded (of the truth)? Nay, but ye are froward folk

36:20.ar: وَجَآءَ مِنۡ أَقۡصَا ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ رَجُلࣱ يَسۡعَىٰ قَالَ يَٰقَوۡمِ ٱتَّبِعُواْ ٱلۡمُرۡسَلِينَ
36:20.en: And there came from the uttermost part of the city a man running. He cried: O my people! Follow those who have been sent

36:21.ar: ٱتَّبِعُواْ مَن لَّا يَسۡـَٔلُكُمۡ أَجۡرࣰ ا وَهُم مُّهۡتَدُونَ
36:21.en: Follow those who ask of you no fee, and who are rightly guided

36:22.ar: وَمَالِيَ لَآ أَعۡبُدُ ٱلَّذِي فَطَرَنِي وَإِلَيۡهِ تُرۡجَعُونَ
36:22.en: For what cause should I not serve Him Who hath created me, and unto Whom ye will be brought back

36:23.ar: ءَأَتَّخِذُ مِن دُونِهِۦٓ ءَالِهَةً إِن يُرِدۡنِ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنُ بِضُرࣲّ لَّا تُغۡنِ عَنِّي شَفَٰعَتُهُمۡ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا وَلَا يُنقِذُونِ
36:23.en: Shall I take (other) gods in place of Him when, if the Beneficent should wish me any harm, their intercession will avail me naught, nor can they save

36:24.ar: إِنِّيٓ إِذࣰ ا لَّفِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينٍ
36:24.en: Then truly I should be in error manifest

36:25.en: Lo! I have believed in your Lord, so hear me

36:26.ar: قِيلَ ٱدۡخُلِ ٱلۡجَنَّةَۖ قَالَ يَٰلَيۡتَ قَوۡمِي يَعۡلَمُونَ
36:26.en: It was said (unto him): Enter paradise. He said: Would that my people knew

36:27.ar: بِمَا غَفَرَ لِي رَبِّي وَجَعَلَنِي مِنَ ٱلۡمُكۡرَمِينَ
36:27.en: With what (munificence) my Lord hath pardoned me and made me of the honoured ones

36:28.ar: ۞وَمَآ أَنزَلۡنَا عَلَىٰ قَوۡمِهِۦ مِنۢ بَعۡدِهِۦ مِن جُندࣲ مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَمَا كُنَّا مُنزِلِينَ
36:28.en: We sent not down against his people after him a host from heaven, nor do We ever send

36:29.ar: إِن كَانَتۡ إِلَّا صَيۡحَةࣰ وَٰحِدَةࣰ فَإِذَا هُمۡ خَٰمِدُونَ
36:29.en: It was but one Shout, and lo! they were extinct

36:30.ar: يَٰحَسۡرَةً عَلَى ٱلۡعِبَادِۚ مَا يَأۡتِيهِم مِّن رَّسُولٍ إِلَّا كَانُواْ بِهِۦ يَسۡتَهۡزِءُونَ
36:30.en: Ah, the anguish for the bondmen! Never came there unto them a messenger but they did mock him

36:31.ar: أَلَمۡ يَرَوۡاْ كَمۡ أَهۡلَكۡنَا قَبۡلَهُم مِّنَ ٱلۡقُرُونِ أَنَّهُمۡ إِلَيۡهِمۡ لَا يَرۡجِعُونَ
36:31.en: Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, which indeed returned not unto them

36:32.ar: وَإِن كُلࣱّ لَّمَّا جَمِيعࣱ لَّدَيۡنَا مُحۡضَرُونَ
36:32.en: But all, without exception, will be brought before Us

7:131.ar: فَإِذَا جَآءَتۡهُمُ ٱلۡحَسَنَةُ قَالُواْ لَنَا هَٰذِهِۦۖ وَإِن تُصِبۡهُمۡ سَيِّئَةࣱ يَطَّيَّرُواْ بِمُوسَىٰ وَمَن مَّعَهُۥٓۗ أَلَآ إِنَّمَا طَٰٓئِرُهُمۡ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
7:131.en: But whenever good befell them, they said: This is ours; and whenever evil smote them they ascribed it to the evil auspices of Moses and those with him. Surely their evil auspice was only with Allah. But most of them knew not

I6u2ikWNuks.title: The Story of the People of the Town (Surah Yasin)
I6u2ikWNuks.one_line: The three messengers and the man who came running in Yasin 13-32, with lessons on superstition, paid religion and belonging to your people.
I6u2ikWNuks.summary: He opens by noting that the Quran calls the setting a city of mixed peoples, and offers his own historical reading: a region around ancient Antioch under a first-century-BC king of mixed Greek-Persian descent who claimed divinity, built a temple of colossal statues on Mount Nemrut, and vanished from the record. He doubts the common view that the messengers were apostles of Isa. Moving through the verses, he explains that people reject a single Lord because idols and middlemen give clergy and rulers power and money. The charge that the messengers are a bad omen leads to a long warning about superstition in Muslim communities: blaming jinn, envy and the evil eye, running to holy men for ruqyah, and denying the mentally ill proper medical care. Ruqyah is for parents to do at home daily, alongside treatment. He contrasts this with the messengers' reply that the people's problem is their own extravagance. The man who runs from the edge of the city argues that the messengers ask no wage, prompting reflection on how imams are paid. His defining word is 'my people': he felt he belonged, had every excuse to stay out, and still spoke, and even after being killed wished his people knew. He asks the community for more people like him.

outline.heading: Opening
Qaryah: a town of mixed peoples
outline.gist: The Quranic word describes a populated place whose people come from different backgrounds, not a single-tribe village.

outline.heading: His historical reading: greater Antioch and a mixed-lineage king
outline.gist: The wider historical Antioch region and a Greek-Persian-Armenian king of the first century BC fit the setting, about a century before Isa.

outline.heading: Mount Nemrut and a kingdom that vanished
outline.gist: The king built a temple of giant statues and claimed divine lineage, then he and his people disappear from history without explanation, which Yasin may account for.

outline.heading: Not the apostles of Isa
outline.gist: Tafsir reports naming them as Isa's disciples lack evidence; the Quran calls them messengers, a term too strong for the apostles.

outline.heading: Two messengers, reinforced by a third
outline.gist: Sending several messengers to one people at once is nearly unique in the Quran; they confirmed one another, each with his own signs.

outline.heading: 'You are only human': why people want middlemen
outline.gist: One Creator gives no one power or profit, so clergy and rulers invent intermediaries and idols that sell blessings and bend the rules.

outline.heading: The messengers' duty is only to convey
outline.gist: They cannot coerce anyone; the grand temple and its spectacle held the people, who are easily dazzled by size and lights.

outline.heading: 'You are a bad omen': shirk breeds superstition
outline.gist: Associating partners with Allah fills a community with superstition, and Muslims who keep this up will lose their children's faith.

outline.heading: Ruqyah belongs in the home
outline.gist: Ruqyah is fully Islamic and parents should recite it daily over their own families instead of seeking holy men with blessed hands or jugs of water.

outline.heading: Mental illness needs a doctor, not a jinn diagnosis
outline.gist: Just as a broken leg goes to hospital, a broken mind needs a professional; diagnosing jinn, magic or envy is ignorance that harms the sick.

outline.heading: Superstition in the Sunnah and in village life
outline.gist: The Prophet taught that linking unrelated events to good or bad luck is not part of the deen; he recalls a villager shunned for supposedly bringing the evil eye.

outline.heading: The omen charge as a substitute for argument
outline.gist: Calling someone a bad omen answers nothing, yet it is persuasive; Musa's people used the same words.

outline.heading: Pseudo-science and the threat of stoning
outline.gist: Talk of dark energy and auras is the modern form of the omen charge; the people threatened to stone and punish the messengers.

outline.heading: 'Your omen is with you': the real cause is extravagance
outline.gist: The messengers turn it back: their troubles come from their own wastefulness and mismanagement, not from those reminding them.

outline.heading: Why the man is left unnamed
outline.gist: Reports naming him come from the People of the Book; what Allah leaves out is left out on purpose so we focus on the lesson.

outline.heading: A man came running from the far end of the city
outline.gist: He hurried in to call his people to follow the messengers.

outline.heading: Follow those who ask no wage
outline.gist: Prophets repeatedly refuse payment; he suggests the way imams are paid deserves rethinking because asking for wealth affects sincerity.

outline.heading: Why would I not worship the One who created me?
outline.gist: The messengers are guided and purposeful; false gods cannot intercede or save; the Quran moves straight to his being told to enter Paradise.

outline.heading: Yasin speaks of the life of the spirit
outline.gist: He ran despite three prophets being present because a living heart cannot bear to see people miss the truth; that is the life Yasin is about.

outline.heading: He had every excuse to stay out
outline.gist: He lived on the outskirts, the people were hostile, three prophets were already on the job and his life was at risk, yet he spoke.

outline.heading: 'My people': belonging and wishing them good
outline.gist: Killed for his call, he still wished his people knew how his Lord forgave and honoured him, because he felt they were his own.

outline.heading: We need more people like him
outline.gist: Every community needs people who feel ownership of the deen, give their time, and hold no grudge.

outline.heading: One cry, and the town was silent
outline.gist: No army was sent, only a single blast, which may explain the missing historical record; all will be brought back for judgment.

outline.heading: Outro

3:103.ar: وَٱعۡتَصِمُواْ بِحَبۡلِ ٱللَّهِ جَمِيعࣰ ا وَلَا تَفَرَّقُواْۚ وَٱذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَتَ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكُمۡ إِذۡ كُنتُمۡ أَعۡدَآءࣰ فَأَلَّفَ بَيۡنَ قُلُوبِكُمۡ فَأَصۡبَحۡتُم بِنِعۡمَتِهِۦٓ إِخۡوَٰنࣰ ا وَكُنتُمۡ عَلَىٰ شَفَا حُفۡرَةࣲ مِّنَ ٱلنَّارِ فَأَنقَذَكُم مِّنۡهَاۗ كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَهۡتَدُونَ
3:103.en: And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate. And remember Allah's favour unto you: How ye were enemies and He made friendship between your hearts so that ye became as brothers by His grace; and (how) ye were upon the brink of an abyss of fire, and He did save you from it. Thus Allah maketh clear His revelations unto you, that haply ye may be guided

3:110.ar: كُنتُمۡ خَيۡرَ أُمَّةٍ أُخۡرِجَتۡ لِلنَّاسِ تَأۡمُرُونَ بِٱلۡمَعۡرُوفِ وَتَنۡهَوۡنَ عَنِ ٱلۡمُنكَرِ وَتُؤۡمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِۗ وَلَوۡ ءَامَنَ أَهۡلُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ لَكَانَ خَيۡرࣰ ا لَّهُمۚ مِّنۡهُمُ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ وَأَكۡثَرُهُمُ ٱلۡفَٰسِقُونَ
3:110.en: Ye are the best community that hath been raised up for mankind. Ye enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency; and ye believe in Allah. And if the People of the Scripture had believed it had been better for them. Some of them are believers; but most of them are evil-livers

9:111.ar: ۞إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ٱشۡتَرَىٰ مِنَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ أَنفُسَهُمۡ وَأَمۡوَٰلَهُم بِأَنَّ لَهُمُ ٱلۡجَنَّةَۚ يُقَٰتِلُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَيَقۡتُلُونَ وَيُقۡتَلُونَۖ وَعۡدًا عَلَيۡهِ حَقࣰّ ا فِي ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةِ وَٱلۡإِنجِيلِ وَٱلۡقُرۡءَانِۚ وَمَنۡ أَوۡفَىٰ بِعَهۡدِهِۦ مِنَ ٱللَّهِۚ فَٱسۡتَبۡشِرُواْ بِبَيۡعِكُمُ ٱلَّذِي بَايَعۡتُم بِهِۦۚ وَذَٰلِكَ هُوَ ٱلۡفَوۡزُ ٱلۡعَظِيمُ
9:111.en: Lo! Allah hath bought from the believers their lives and their wealth because the Garden will be theirs: they shall fight in the way of Allah and shall slay and be slain. It is a promise which is binding on Him in the Torah and the Gospel and the Qur'an. Who fulfilleth His covenant better than Allah? Rejoice then in your bargain that ye have made, for that is the supreme triumph

Zsqsp2DDLXg.speaker_note: Sheikh's voice: tells of running a village masjid at 17 and of the earlier survey he ran before founding the centre.
Zsqsp2DDLXg.title: London Muslim Survey (Part 2)
Zsqsp2DDLXg.one_line: Using survey findings, he calls on the missing 30-to-50-year-olds to give time, not just money, and lists the community's gaps in marriage, finances and mental health.
Zsqsp2DDLXg.summary: He starts from the command to hold together to the rope of Allah and the description of the ummah that enjoins good. Enjoining the good, he argues, is social maintenance, not da'wah: Muslims should find the good values a society already holds, like caring for elders, the vulnerable and equality, and strengthen them. Reform is for where the society is wrong. The London Muslim Survey helps with that. His own ten-year observation is that masjids have children, young adults and the elderly but almost no one aged 30 to 50 outside the boards, so boys have no men to learn from. The Prophet engaged every age group, and the companions all opened their homes. The story of Abu Bakr secretly cleaning and cooking for a blind old woman while he was caliph shows that no position exempts anyone from basic service. Influence often comes from one small encounter, as when al-Sha'bi urged a young Abu Hanifa to seek knowledge. He then goes through the slides: newcomers struggling financially in years three to six, a growing marriage crisis made worse by parents' costs and racism, parents struggling to pass on Islamic identity, untreated mental illness replaced by ruqyah from strangers, no support for people facing discrimination, and isolated converts. He frames it all as Allah's transaction: give your life, time and wealth, and receive Paradise.

outline.heading: Opening
Hold the rope together
outline.gist: Scholars differ on whether the rope of Allah is the Quran, the deen, the Prophet or each other, and any reading leads to the same place; the word that matters is the one after it: together, as a group, not divided.

outline.heading: Ma'ruf is social maintenance, not da'wah
outline.gist: 3:110: commanding ma'ruf is social rather than religious in nature. Da'wah teaches the deen; ma'ruf maintains a society by evaluating its norms, affirming what people rightly see as good and bad, and saving reform and argument for where the society is wrong.

outline.heading: Strengthen the good values a society already holds
outline.gist: Muslims arriving in a society should identify its good values, such as caring for elders and the vulnerable, equality and diversity, even when poorly implemented, and make them stronger; we mostly do the other half, pointing out what must change.

outline.heading: Where we agree, and where reform needs arguments
outline.gist: Society may not call drugs haram but still discourages them, so we stand with it. Where we disagree, we need sound arguments and a platform to challenge the norm by bringing Allah's narrative into the arena.

outline.heading: Why the survey: know what is happening first
outline.gist: You cannot strengthen what works or change what does not without knowing a community's values, norms and customs; the survey data serves that purpose.

outline.heading: Missing age groups, and the Prophet's wide circle
outline.gist: Over ten years he has seen whole age groups missing from volunteering and work in Islamic institutions. The Prophet invested in teens, people in their thirties and forties and elders alike, which is why his impact spread so quickly.

outline.heading: The village masjid he ran at seventeen
outline.gist: An old stone masjid that everyone had left for a newer one was handed to him at seventeen; it was full of schoolchildren and grandfathers, and he grew up thinking that was normal.

outline.heading: No men for boys to learn from
outline.gist: Today he has people in their early twenties, children and elders, but those aged 30 to 50 only sit on boards. He does not know how boys will learn to be men with only two or three men around.

outline.heading: Can't you carve out an hour a week?
outline.gist: Same-age groups left to themselves do not grow well. Busy people always answer 'when I have time', yet cannot spare an hour or two a week simply to be among people and help them; he has preached mentorship for seven years.

outline.heading: Time and experience, not just wealth
outline.gist: Without people of every age giving time, expertise and experience, we will not get far. The Prophet made the companions do things that before Islam were beneath men of their age, wealth and standing.

outline.heading: The Prophet engaged every demographic
outline.gist: He spent hours helping elderly women, went into the alleys to ask children about their pets and birds, and sat with the poorest who lived in the masjid.

outline.heading: Every companion opened his home
outline.gist: No one was exempt: even those who could buy a house for someone still had to take people into their own. The standard exposed the hypocrites by their own choices.

outline.heading: Your share is your time, not just your money
outline.gist: He knows people are busy, but showing up and helping is part of what you owe, and the community is not doing well on money either.

outline.heading: Umar follows Abu Bakr to the blind woman's house
outline.gist: While ruling a vast empire, Abu Bakr disappeared on the same day every week. Umar followed him, feared the worst, and found a blind old woman whose house a stranger had been cleaning, mending and cooking for. Umar wept: you have made it impossible for those after you.

outline.heading: A spot waiting for you down in the mud
outline.gist: Even the supreme leader still has a place on the ground with those who struggle. No PhD, title or signature makes you bigger than Abu Bakr.

outline.heading: Umar and the child's bird
outline.gist: By his telling, Umar objected when he saw the Prophet with six-year-olds while there was work to do, and was told the child's little bird had died that day. It made sense to him only later.

outline.heading: Expertise, plus simply showing up
outline.gist: Contribute through your profession, but also through basic presence: prayers, small chances to volunteer with young people. The missing middle generation fills boards but nothing else, and four or five people cannot mentor a whole community.

outline.heading: These are not like us; these are us
outline.gist: Images from Rafah and Gaza are beyond heartbreaking, and the world has openly chosen to look away. The people dying there are us, and the ummah is nowhere near able to push back against this tide.

outline.heading: Influence starts small
outline.gist: Change starts with an hour helping kids, a homeless shelter or a soup kitchen. Ask successful people what moved them and they name one small moment, not years of lectures.

outline.heading: Al-Sha'bi and the young Abu Hanifa
outline.gist: Abu Hanifa said what changed him was Imam al-Sha'bi asking the young market trader whom he studied with and telling him not to waste such a mind. Had al-Sha'bi been too busy for the youth, we would have lost one of our greatest imams.

outline.heading: Survey: newcomers forgotten after year three
outline.gist: Newcomers are supported for a year or two, then drift and are forgotten, struggling between years three and six. A family that cannot make ends meet cannot take care of itself spiritually, socially or ethically.

outline.heading: Survey: more unmarried past 25 and 35
outline.gist: The number of unmarried young men and women past 25, 30 and 35 is far beyond what any community has seen, and those who marry struggle to sustain it.

outline.heading: Parents' costly cultural blockades
outline.gist: Working with singles changes little while parents keep marriage expensive and put cultural obstacles in its way; the whole community will feel it within a generation.

outline.heading: When haram becomes easy
outline.gist: Some companions were so poor they considered castrating themselves; people today will not, because haram is too easy. Once haram is normalized in a community, there is little point remaining in it.

outline.heading: Racism in the ummah of Muhammad
outline.gist: Besides lack of support and money, some say they cannot marry because of racial barriers.

outline.heading: Parents struggling to pass on Islamic identity
outline.gist: Parents struggle to make their children proud of being Muslim, a sign the community is not functioning: a healthy one gives its youth every reason to feel they belong.

outline.heading: Why he focuses on what is not working
outline.gist: His pessimism is about the numbers, not the people: what works will keep working, but these gaps hurt people and nothing stands between us and fixing them except our own commitment.

outline.heading: Ask, gather, plan: everyone is responsible
outline.gist: His earlier survey found Islamic knowledge was what parents most wanted, so a place was founded to teach it. Communities should ask, gather information and plan to close the gaps, and everyone shares responsibility for meeting them.

outline.heading: Allah's transaction
outline.gist: Allah asks for your life, time and wealth and gives Paradise in return; if you accept the deal, all of this makes sense.

outline.heading: Mental illness is underreported
outline.gist: The survey reached people already in the masjid, so the real numbers are higher; a barrier in the community keeps people from reaching professionals in time.

outline.heading: Ruqyah is not a substitute for a broken leg
outline.gist: He does ruqyah for his family every night as sunnah, but replacing mental health care with ruqyah from a stranger is foreign to the deen. You take a broken leg to a doctor; do the same for depression and anxiety.

outline.heading: No support for those facing discrimination
outline.gist: People targeted at school, university or work for their faith, appearance or dress should know where to go and find proper support; the community has not built that.

outline.heading: Isolation, especially for converts
outline.gist: Open-ended answers spoke of social isolation, especially among converts who do not know whom to turn to.

outline.heading: Outro

62:9.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ إِذَا نُودِيَ لِلصَّلَوٰةِ مِن يَوۡمِ ٱلۡجُمُعَةِ فَٱسۡعَوۡاْ إِلَىٰ ذِكۡرِ ٱللَّهِ وَذَرُواْ ٱلۡبَيۡعَۚ ذَٰلِكُمۡ خَيۡرࣱ لَّكُمۡ إِن كُنتُمۡ تَعۡلَمُونَ
62:9.en: O ye who believe! When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading. That is better for you if ye did but know

62:10.ar: فَإِذَا قُضِيَتِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةُ فَٱنتَشِرُواْ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَٱبۡتَغُواْ مِن فَضۡلِ ٱللَّهِ وَٱذۡكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيرࣰ ا لَّعَلَّكُمۡ تُفۡلِحُونَ
62:10.en: And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty, and remember Allah much, that ye may be successful

62:11.ar: وَإِذَا رَأَوۡاْ تِجَٰرَةً أَوۡ لَهۡوًا ٱنفَضُّوٓاْ إِلَيۡهَا وَتَرَكُوكَ قَآئِمࣰ اۚ قُلۡ مَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ خَيۡرࣱ مِّنَ ٱللَّهۡوِ وَمِنَ ٱلتِّجَٰرَةِۚ وَٱللَّهُ خَيۡرُ ٱلرَّٰزِقِينَ
62:11.en: But when they spy some merchandise or pastime they break away to it and leave thee standing. Say: That which Allah hath is better than pastime and than merchandise, and Allah is the Best of providers

62:5.ar: مَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ حُمِّلُواْ ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةَ ثُمَّ لَمۡ يَحۡمِلُوهَا كَمَثَلِ ٱلۡحِمَارِ يَحۡمِلُ أَسۡفَارَۢاۚ بِئۡسَ مَثَلُ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلَّذِينَ كَذَّبُواْ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۚ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
62:5.en: The likeness of those who are entrusted with the Law of Moses, yet apply it not, is as the likeness of the ass carrying books. Wretched is the likeness of folk who deny the revelations of Allah. And Allah guideth not wrongdoing folk

62:6.ar: قُلۡ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ هَادُوٓاْ إِن زَعَمۡتُمۡ أَنَّكُمۡ أَوۡلِيَآءُ لِلَّهِ مِن دُونِ ٱلنَّاسِ فَتَمَنَّوُاْ ٱلۡمَوۡتَ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
62:6.en: Say (O Muhammad): O ye who are Jews! If ye claim that ye are favoured of Allah apart from (all) mankind, then long for death if ye are truthful

62:7.ar: وَلَا يَتَمَنَّوۡنَهُۥٓ أَبَدَۢا بِمَا قَدَّمَتۡ أَيۡدِيهِمۡۚ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمُۢ بِٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
62:7.en: But they will never long for it because of all that their own hands have sent before, and Allah is Aware of evil-doers

62:8.ar: قُلۡ إِنَّ ٱلۡمَوۡتَ ٱلَّذِي تَفِرُّونَ مِنۡهُ فَإِنَّهُۥ مُلَٰقِيكُمۡۖ ثُمَّ تُرَدُّونَ إِلَىٰ عَٰلِمِ ٱلۡغَيۡبِ وَٱلشَّهَٰدَةِ فَيُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ

Rbqi7mhnXTI.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Jumuah 62:9-11 (Part 4)
Rbqi7mhnXTI.one_line: The closing verses of Al-Jumuah are addressed to the attendees: hasten to Jumuah, follow and question your leadership, and never leave the khatib standing alone.
Rbqi7mhnXTI.summary: Closing Surat Al-Jumuah, he first restates his reading of the surah in a long review: Jumuah is the leadership system Allah built into the religion. Muslims have neutralized it by turning the khatib into a salaried employee of a board with no vision of his own. The person on the minbar should either be the community's leader or speak openly on that leader's behalf. The earlier verses addressed the khatib. These final three address the congregation, whose duty is to be willing to be led, to follow, to give feedback and to hold leaders accountable. Western masjids have no excuse, because no regime scripts their sermons. On 62:9 he stresses that Jumuah is obligatory for resident men, criticizes the laxity that followed Covid, and cites the severe hadith on missing it. He explains the call to hasten and to leave all trade, including the trade of selling oneself. On 62:10 he says the masjid is not a place to stay: go out, seek Allah's bounty, and act on what you learned while remembering Him. On 62:11 he tells the story of the caravan that drew people away while the Prophet stood on the minbar. He reads 'standing' as carrying a burden alone, and says no imam can carry the religion by himself.

outline.heading: Opening
A simple surah: Jumuah organizes the ummah
outline.gist: The surah organizes leadership simply: each week the leader stands on the minbar, says what comes next and revises the plan, and the men who attend inform their families.

outline.heading: Neutralized, but still alive
outline.gist: Muslims have neutralized Jumuah almost everywhere, yet reviving it would change their state quickly because it still exists and even those far from Allah attend. It only needs a worthy message from someone with authority to lead; he himself has no wish to lead.

outline.heading: The leader, or someone clearly speaking for him
outline.gist: As a young man he gave khutbahs for his elderly teacher, who still led the community. A khatib employed by a board to hit its milestones is a puppet with no vision; today's Jumuah is neither the leader nor his spokesman, just a lecture on steroids.

outline.heading: A community that meets weekly cannot fail
outline.gist: Once people stop finding benefit they stop coming, yet a community whose leader tells it every week where it is going, and which follows up and gives feedback, can hardly fail.

outline.heading: The first page addressed the khatib
outline.gist: The earlier verses chastise the speaker: if he fails to teach responsibility instead of favour and to remind people of death, the congregation becomes a donkey carrying books. The final verses address the attendees.

outline.heading: Being willing to be led
outline.gist: Attendees are part of the fabric of Jumuah: it needs someone to lead and people willing to be led. That does not mean surrendering autonomy, and no one is obeyed in disobedience to Allah.

outline.heading: Following only your own direction makes you the leader
outline.gist: Walking behind a leader only when he goes your way is not followship. Trust a reasoned direction, and if it proves wrong the weekly Jumuah will correct it; anything beats being a headless chicken.

outline.heading: Poor followers are part of the problem
outline.gist: He calls himself a decorated complainer. Blame imams and boards all you like, but a poor follower is part of the problem; at work you are not always the leader either, and that lessens no one.

outline.heading: Follow, give feedback, hold accountable: the Prophet's weekly loop
outline.gist: Jumuah is a two-way road: one person speaks, everyone listens, and feedback comes through the week so the next khutbah responds to it. That loop is how the Prophet grew his community.

outline.heading: No regime scripts our khutbahs
outline.gist: In Syria or Egypt a totalitarian regime hands the imam a script he cannot leave. Here masajid have autonomy, so the only barrier to proper leadership is ourselves.

outline.heading: Large US masajid and a clear structure
outline.gist: Some very large American masajid thrive because everyone, the imam included, knows who makes the calls. An imam need not lead, only know who his leader is so he can move people in that direction.

outline.heading: Reciting 62:9-11, and the connecting hamza
outline.gist: He introduces the final passage as addressed to attendees and followers, recites it, and notes that a connecting hamza is pronounced only when starting from it and drops in continuous reading.

outline.heading: The first call to the believers
outline.gist: Until now the surah did not address the believers; it described Allah's attributes, the purpose of prophets and what happens when leaders fail. This passage is for the attendee.

outline.heading: Favoured or responsible?
outline.gist: Feeling favoured by Allah and feeling responsible to Him are easily confused but opposite: the first leads to rock bottom, the second motivates you to use what you were given.

outline.heading: When the call is made on Friday
outline.gist: The call meant is the Friday prayer, which the Prophet always held in place of Dhuhr; the verse need not say so because his practice settles it.

outline.heading: No adhan in the street: plan for Jumuah
outline.gist: Back home you hear the adhan and close your shop. Here you must set reminders, arrange time with your employer, find the nearest Jumuah and transport, and that extra effort is obligatory.

outline.heading: An obligation for men, despite the post-COVID slide
outline.gist: After COVID young men grew lax about Jumuah. It is optional for women but mandatory for every resident man, with no exception but illness or travel.

outline.heading: Whatever the quality of the khutbah
outline.gist: A surgeon mid-operation or a pilot may be excused, but otherwise you attend even if the khatib speaks Klingon to people from Mars: praise Allah, pray and leave.

outline.heading: The threat to burn houses
outline.gist: The Prophet said he had intended to have wood gathered and burn the houses of Muslim men who stay away from Jumuah; such strict language from him signals something major.

outline.heading: Harsh warnings mark a system, not only a ritual
outline.gist: Whoever misses three in a row without excuse has his heart turned away. Like zakah, the ummah's financial backbone that Abu Bakr fought to keep, Jumuah is a leadership system, and abandoning it rips the ummah's fabric.

outline.heading: Hasten with tunnel vision
outline.gist: Fas'aw means moving quickly and forcefully, dropping everything with tunnel vision toward the remembrance of Allah, where you hear what He wants from you and for you.

outline.heading: Remembering Allah as a community
outline.gist: An individual can worship alone, but a community praises Allah by knowing where it is going, picking up its pace, caring for its vulnerable and solving its acute and chronic problems.

outline.heading: Leave all selling, including selling yourself
outline.gist: Every person goes out each morning selling himself, freeing or ruining himself. Leave every transaction, whether goods, tuition or hours for a paycheck.

outline.heading: Better for you, if you knew
outline.gist: Nothing is more valuable than having Jumuah. At 38 he has spent twenty years trying to work out how to fix it, when the solution is already built in.

outline.heading: Disperse and seek Allah's bounty
outline.gist: Allah fills the masjid on Friday because He calls the people. When the prayer ends, go out: masajid are not places to stay all day, and there is work to do while remembering Allah much.

outline.heading: Take the week's lesson out with you
outline.gist: Do not seek your livelihood and forget Allah until next Friday; carry the remembrance you were given and act on what you learned that week.

outline.heading: That you may succeed, as a community
outline.gist: Success comes when people attend faithfully, hear a direction from the minbar, and spend the week pursuing it while remembering Allah.

outline.heading: A verse that made his teachers weep
outline.gist: Some of his teachers could not recite this verse without tears. When people see a profitable deal or some amusement, lesser priorities than Jumuah, they rush toward it.

outline.heading: The caravan during the khutbah
outline.gist: Infaddu means pushing and shoving to get out. Early in Medina a trading caravan arrived while the Prophet was on the minbar, and because goods were scarce people ran out to buy, leaving him standing; the verse came down about this.

outline.heading: Standing: carrying the burden alone
outline.gist: Qa'im in the Quran means taking a stand and carrying its burden, not just being upright, so they left him carrying the responsibility alone.

outline.heading: What is with Allah is better
outline.gist: What Allah holds for you through this system beats any amusement or deal, and He is the best of providers, so missing the first bid is no loss. Do not leave the speaker standing while you walk out.

outline.heading: No khatib can carry the deen alone
outline.gist: If the person on the minbar carries the religion alone it is a disaster; everyone must share the ownership. The Prophet did not stop the khutbah to follow them, so if the speaker is still speaking you are still listening.

outline.heading: Jumuah as a symbolic commitment
outline.gist: Attending is a symbolic commitment to the nation and its leadership. The argument is hard to make when Jumuah has become a token, yet in Islam you cannot stop your part because others do theirs badly.

outline.heading: In Islam you always do your part
outline.gist: Attend whether the imam is good or bad or shouts a lot, look for better if you can, and attend anyway if you cannot; then hold leaders accountable for offering direction worth following.

outline.heading: Replace khatibs who give no direction
outline.gist: Speakers who offer no direction should be replaced, and that is the attendees' responsibility too. Board members are ordinary people who ran for a position; know your place, but make sure the right person is on the minbar.

outline.heading: Staying gains more than leaving
outline.gist: What Allah has planned for a united ummah with direction outweighs an extra hour of work. A student with an exam has an excuse, but most absences come from not taking it seriously.

outline.heading: Questioning followers keep leaders sharp
outline.gist: Young men usually know when they could have made it. Followers must be part of the accountability system: questions can be annoying, but a leader nobody questions becomes lazy and says anything.

outline.heading: Outro

JW9TPthJdbg.title: Ramadan Prep: The Bounties of Ramadan
JW9TPthJdbg.one_line: The Prophet's pre-Ramadan sermon explained, then five bounties to aim for: forgiveness, freedom from the Fire, immense reward, Laylat al-Qadr and answered dua.
JW9TPthJdbg.summary: He explains the long narration of the Prophet's sermon before Ramadan, noting that scholars dispute its chain but accept its meaning. Each phrase becomes a lesson: a voluntary deed in Ramadan equals an obligation, and nothing outweighs an obligation; it is the month of patience, rewarded with Paradise without reckoning, where patience means holding a high standard rather than having a hard life; the month of empathy, since hunger teaches what the poor feel, as the Prophet and companions bound stones to their stomachs; provision grows because appreciation grows, which he ties to watching people starved on screens while the ummah fails its duty; and feeding the fasting was meant first for those with nothing. He then sets out five bounties to aim for. Forgiveness of sins through fasting, night prayer and Laylat al-Qadr offers a clean slate. Freedom from the Fire is granted every night on merit, the moment the Prophet sought most. Fasting's reward is beyond numbers, but only if one avoids haram while abstaining from halal. Laylat al-Qadr teaches quality over quantity, centres on the Quran and is spoiled by quarrels. The fasting person's dua is answered, so he urges people to learn to speak to Allah humbly and without formality.

outline.heading: Opening
Know the bounties so you have a target
outline.gist: Ramadan brings a closeness and serenity found at no other time; knowing its five bounties gives you something to aim for all month.

outline.heading: The Prophet's sermon before Ramadan
outline.gist: The narration's chain is disputed but its meaning is accepted by scholars and his teachers; the Prophet stood on the minbar days before Ramadan, and Arabs distinguished such an oration from a seated talk.

outline.heading: A great month with a night of a thousand months
outline.gist: Fasting its days is obligatory, praying its nights voluntary, and any good deed in it counts as an obligation done elsewhere.

outline.heading: Why equalling an obligation matters
outline.gist: All voluntary deeds ever done do not equal one obligation, and a missed obligation's reward is never recovered; in Ramadan one obligation counts as seventy.

outline.heading: The month of patience: Paradise without reckoning
outline.gist: Standing before Allah to account for youth, wealth and time is the hardest moment of existence; the patient are spared it entirely.

outline.heading: What patience really means
outline.gist: Patience is not having a hard life but setting a high standard and persevering toward it; Ramadan is hard by design and its reward is Paradise.

outline.heading: The month of empathy
outline.gist: Fasting voluntarily teaches what involuntary hunger feels like, just as recovered addicts make the best counsellors.

outline.heading: Months without a cooking fire
outline.gist: The Prophet's household went months on dates and water; companions bound stones to their stomachs, which shrinks the stomach's pouch and dulls hunger, as gastric bypass does.

outline.heading: One stone each, and the Prophet's two
outline.gist: Three hungry young men showed the Prophet the stones on their bellies; he smiled and showed two on his own.

outline.heading: Do not spend Ramadan feeling sorry for yourself
outline.gist: You will be fine at sunset; let the month strengthen empathy for those who will not, so that you give more.

outline.heading: Provision increases through appreciation
outline.gist: His bank balance never grew in Ramadan; what grows is gratitude, as hunger makes an old car and a modest income look like plenty.

outline.heading: Starvation broadcast on our screens
outline.gist: There is money to film people starving to death but not to feed them; the brutality against the people of the Holy Land should make this Ramadan a turning point.

outline.heading: The ummah has not done its job
outline.gist: Such disregard for Muslim life shows Muslims have neglected their purpose and responsibilities; feel it as you break a fast others cannot.

outline.heading: Entitled children and entitled servants
outline.gist: Parents are worn out by children who always want more; Allah sees us the same way, and we forget that what we have could be much less.

outline.heading: Feeding the fasting person
outline.gist: Whoever gives iftar earns the faster's reward; family iftars are good, but the Prophet meant first those who could not otherwise break their fast; the month runs from mercy to forgiveness to freedom from the Fire.

outline.heading: Bounty one: forgiveness of sins
outline.gist: Believers feel the weight of their shortcomings rather than comparing themselves with the public, so a wiped slate matters most to them.

outline.heading: Fasting with faith and hope of reward
outline.gist: Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward has his past sins forgiven.

outline.heading: Night prayer, Laylat al-Qadr and a greyed-out record
outline.gist: Standing its nights or Laylat al-Qadr also forgives past sins; imagine your record with the bad deeds still there but stamped forgiven.

outline.heading: Allah offers a fresh start
outline.gist: It is as if Allah says let us begin again; He loves to forgive where people do not, so missing it is a real loss.

outline.heading: Three 'ameens' on the minbar
outline.gist: Jibril prayed against whoever reaches Ramadan and is not forgiven; with so many routes to forgiveness, missing them takes effort.

outline.heading: Bounty two: freedom from the Fire
outline.gist: Like freeing a slave, Allah breaks the chain that binds a person to Hell, and He frees people every night of Ramadan.

outline.heading: Not a lottery but merit
outline.gist: More are freed in the last ten nights, and being chosen outweighs graduation, marriage, a first child or a dream promotion.

outline.heading: A freedom never revoked
outline.gist: Once granted it is never taken back; you may still sin, but you will always find your way back to Allah and your end will be good.

outline.heading: What the Prophet asked for most
outline.gist: Most of his supplications at the end of Ramadan, rich in glorifying Allah, centred on this; what a loss to pass a Ramadan without it.

outline.heading: Hell paraded on the Day of Judgement
outline.gist: Hell is dragged out by 70,000 reins each held by 70,000 angels, straining to devour; knees buckle and no one dares look straight at it.

outline.heading: Bring your best: there is no nepotism
outline.gist: The freed are far from all of it because they gave their all one night in Ramadan; it is granted on merit.

outline.heading: Bounty three: reward beyond measure
outline.gist: Beyond the multiplied deeds, Allah says every deed has a set reward except fasting, which is His and which He rewards Himself.

outline.heading: The blank line on the billboard
outline.gist: Scanning the reward values for your deeds you find none for fasting, because Allah will reward it personally; a modest effort for us is a great deal to Him.

outline.heading: The red line moves in Ramadan
outline.gist: Fasting pushes you back from even halal food, drink and marital relations, so fighting, cursing or gossiping while fasting makes no sense.

outline.heading: Fasting that yields only hunger
outline.gist: Many get nothing from fasting but hunger and nothing from night prayer but fatigue, because they lacked intention and focus.

outline.heading: Bounty four: Laylat al-Qadr, quality over quantity
outline.gist: Surah al-Qadr came about a decade before fasting was prescribed, teaching that a night can outweigh a thousand months, about 82 years, a whole lifetime.

outline.heading: The Prophet's search and the quarrel
outline.gist: He secluded himself in the first, middle and last ten nights until told it lay in the last ten, then forgot its date while reconciling two men fighting outside the masjid.

outline.heading: Do not spoil it with disputes
outline.gist: The lesson is not to ruin the night by harming people or dividing the community; seek it in the odd nights, counted from the start or the end.

outline.heading: Dedicate all ten nights
outline.gist: Scholars reject betting only on the 27th; it is hidden so we commit to all ten, and a single prostration that night could weigh like 82 years.

outline.heading: The night is about the Quran
outline.gist: It marks the first revelation; Umm Ayman wept that revelation had ended, but each year Jibril descends with the angels to see the Quran alive in the hearts of the ummah.

outline.heading: Peace until dawn
outline.gist: Allah grants peace to all creation that night, so a quarrel ruins it; guard your behaviour in the last ten.

outline.heading: Bounty five: the fasting person's dua
outline.gist: Its acceptance means a response: what you asked, something better later, harm removed, sins forgiven or rank raised, while some duas are thrown back.

outline.heading: Prepare your dua in advance
outline.gist: Use the free dua at iftar; earlier generations prepared and memorised their Ramadan duas months ahead so they were ready in every prostration.

outline.heading: Islam is learning to speak to Allah
outline.gist: Islam teaches who Allah is and how to communicate with Him, a relationship unlike any other we have.

outline.heading: Come without titles
outline.gist: Dua is not a formal interview; in prostration you put your face in the dirt, so come as a weak, scared creature without your degrees or bank balance.

outline.heading: The dua exercise
outline.gist: Say every memorised dua, then sit again and make a second dua without repeating a single word, to learn to speak unmasked.

outline.heading: 2:186: no middleman
outline.gist: When asked about Allah, the verse drops the usual 'say' and Allah answers directly that He is near and responds.

outline.heading: The gates of Heaven open
outline.gist: Ramadan's different feel, impossible to replicate, is because Heaven's gates are open and Hell's are shut.

outline.heading: Devils chained: the sin is yours
outline.gist: With the devils chained, any sin in Ramadan comes from your own nafs, a lesson in telling internal from external sources of sin.

outline.heading: Allah calls the hearts
outline.gist: A caller invites seekers of good to come forward; Allah draws crowds no programme could, and the truly deprived is the one who misses Ramadan's mercy.

quran.point: The Quran was sent down on a night better than a thousand months, revealed years before fasting was prescribed.
The angels and Jibril descend, and the night is peace until dawn.

hadith.gist: The Prophet's sermon before Ramadan: a great month with a night better than a thousand months; a voluntary deed equals an obligation and an obligation equals seventy; the month of patience and of empathy; provision increases; feeding a fasting person earns his reward; its beginning is mercy, middle forgiveness, end freedom from the Fire.
The Prophet's household went months without lighting a fire to cook, living on dates and water.
Companions showed the Prophet a stone tied to each of their stomachs from hunger, and he showed two tied to his.
Whoever gives a fasting person food to break his fast gets his reward without reducing it.
Whoever fasts Ramadan, or stands its nights, or stands Laylat al-Qadr out of faith and seeking reward has his past sins forgiven.
The Prophet said 'ameen' on three steps of the minbar; Jibril had prayed against one who reaches Ramadan and is not forgiven.
Allah frees people from the Fire every night of Ramadan.
Hell is brought on the Day of Judgement with 70,000 reins, each held by 70,000 angels.
Every deed of the son of Adam is for him except fasting; it is for Me and I reward it.
Many who fast get nothing from it but hunger, and many who pray at night get nothing but sleeplessness.
The Prophet secluded himself in the first, then middle, then last ten nights seeking Laylat al-Qadr.
The Prophet came out to tell its date, found two men quarrelling, and the knowledge was lifted; seek it in the odd nights of the last ten.
Umm Ayman wept after the Prophet's death because revelation from heaven had ended.
The fasting person has a supplication at the time of breaking the fast that is not rejected.
In Ramadan the gates of Heaven are opened, the gates of Hell closed and the devils chained.
A caller calls in Ramadan: seeker of good, come forward; seeker of evil, hold back.

9:91.ar: لَّيۡسَ عَلَى ٱلضُّعَفَآءِ وَلَا عَلَى ٱلۡمَرۡضَىٰ وَلَا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يَجِدُونَ مَا يُنفِقُونَ حَرَجٌ إِذَا نَصَحُواْ لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦۚ مَا عَلَى ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ مِن سَبِيلࣲۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
9:91.en: Not unto the weak nor unto the sick nor unto those who can find naught to spend is any fault (to be imputed though they stay at home) if they are true to Allah and His messenger. Not unto the good is there any road (of blame). Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

9:92.ar: وَلَا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا مَآ أَتَوۡكَ لِتَحۡمِلَهُمۡ قُلۡتَ لَآ أَجِدُ مَآ أَحۡمِلُكُمۡ عَلَيۡهِ تَوَلَّواْ وَّأَعۡيُنُهُمۡ تَفِيضُ مِنَ ٱلدَّمۡعِ حَزَنًا أَلَّا يَجِدُواْ مَا يُنفِقُونَ
9:92.en: Nor unto those whom, when they came to thee (asking) that thou shouldst mount them, thou didst tell: I cannot find whereon to mount you. They turned back with eyes flowing with tears, for sorrow that they could not find the means to spend

9:93.ar: ۞إِنَّمَا ٱلسَّبِيلُ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ يَسۡتَـٔۡذِنُونَكَ وَهُمۡ أَغۡنِيَآءُۚ رَضُواْ بِأَن يَكُونُواْ مَعَ ٱلۡخَوَالِفِ وَطَبَعَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمۡ فَهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
9:93.en: The road (of blame) is only against those who ask for leave of thee (to stay at home) when they are rich. They are content to be with the useless. Allah hath sealed their hearts so that they know not

9:94.ar: يَعۡتَذِرُونَ إِلَيۡكُمۡ إِذَا رَجَعۡتُمۡ إِلَيۡهِمۡۚ قُل لَّا تَعۡتَذِرُواْ لَن نُّؤۡمِنَ لَكُمۡ قَدۡ نَبَّأَنَا ٱللَّهُ مِنۡ أَخۡبَارِكُمۡۚ وَسَيَرَى ٱللَّهُ عَمَلَكُمۡ وَرَسُولُهُۥ ثُمَّ تُرَدُّونَ إِلَىٰ عَٰلِمِ ٱلۡغَيۡبِ وَٱلشَّهَٰدَةِ فَيُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
9:94.en: They will make excuse to you (Muslims) when ye return unto them. Say: Make no excuse, for we shall not believe you. Allah hath told us tidings of you. Allah and His messenger will see your conduct, and then ye will be brought back unto Him Who knoweth the Invisible as well as the Visible, and He will tell you what ye used to do

9:95.ar: سَيَحۡلِفُونَ بِٱللَّهِ لَكُمۡ إِذَا ٱنقَلَبۡتُمۡ إِلَيۡهِمۡ لِتُعۡرِضُواْ عَنۡهُمۡۖ فَأَعۡرِضُواْ عَنۡهُمۡۖ إِنَّهُمۡ رِجۡسࣱۖ وَمَأۡوَىٰهُمۡ جَهَنَّمُ جَزَآءَۢ بِمَا كَانُواْ يَكۡسِبُونَ
9:95.en: They will swear by Allah unto you, when ye return unto them, that ye may let them be. Let them be, for lo! they are unclean, and their abode is hell as the reward for what they used to earn

9:96.ar: يَحۡلِفُونَ لَكُمۡ لِتَرۡضَوۡاْ عَنۡهُمۡۖ فَإِن تَرۡضَوۡاْ عَنۡهُمۡ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَرۡضَىٰ عَنِ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلۡفَٰسِقِينَ
9:96.en: They swear unto you, that ye may accept them. Though ye accept them. Allah verily accepteth not wrongdoing folk

9:117.ar: لَّقَد تَّابَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَى ٱلنَّبِيِّ وَٱلۡمُهَٰجِرِينَ وَٱلۡأَنصَارِ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوهُ فِي سَاعَةِ ٱلۡعُسۡرَةِ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ مَا كَادَ يَزِيغُ قُلُوبُ فَرِيقࣲ مِّنۡهُمۡ ثُمَّ تَابَ عَلَيۡهِمۡۚ إِنَّهُۥ بِهِمۡ رَءُوفࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
9:117.en: Allah hath turned in mercy to the Prophet, and to the Muhajirin and the Ansar who followed him in the hour of hardship. After the hearts of a party of them had almost swerved aside, then turned He unto them in mercy. Lo! He is Full of Pity, Merciful for them

9:118.ar: وَعَلَى ٱلثَّلَٰثَةِ ٱلَّذِينَ خُلِّفُواْ حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا ضَاقَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ بِمَا رَحُبَتۡ وَضَاقَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمۡ أَنفُسُهُمۡ وَظَنُّوٓاْ أَن لَّا مَلۡجَأَ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ إِلَّآ إِلَيۡهِ ثُمَّ تَابَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ لِيَتُوبُوٓاْۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
9:118.en: And to the three also (did He turn in mercy) who were left behind, when the earth, vast as it is, was straitened for them, and their own souls were straitened for them till they bethought them that there is no refuge from Allah save toward Him. Then turned He unto them in mercy that they (too) might turn (repentant unto Him). Lo! Allah! He is the Relenting, the Merciful

9:119.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ ٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَكُونُواْ مَعَ ٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ
9:119.en: O ye who believe! Be careful of your duty to Allah, and be with the truthful

9:80.ar: ٱسۡتَغۡفِرۡ لَهُمۡ أَوۡ لَا تَسۡتَغۡفِرۡ لَهُمۡ إِن تَسۡتَغۡفِرۡ لَهُمۡ سَبۡعِينَ مَرَّةࣰ فَلَن يَغۡفِرَ ٱللَّهُ لَهُمۡۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمۡ كَفَرُواْ بِٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦۗ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلۡفَٰسِقِينَ
9:80.en: Ask forgiveness for them (O Muhammad), or ask not forgiveness for them; though thou ask forgiveness for them seventy times Allah will not forgive them. That is because they disbelieved in Allah and His messenger, and Allah guideth not wrongdoing folk

qFtXNE8yRd4.title: The Expedition of Tabuk and the Story of Ka'b ibn Malik
qFtXNE8yRd4.one_line: Ka'b ibn Malik's staying back from Tabuk, his honesty and fifty-day boycott, and what At-Tawbah teaches about earning a place with the Prophet.
qFtXNE8yRd4.summary: Framed as preparation for Ramadan, he tells the story of Ka'b ibn Malik, mostly in Ka'b's own words from his long narration, alongside the verses of At-Tawbah. He sets the scene: the Prophet openly declared a long march north against Roman-allied forces in the August heat at harvest time, and everyone had to carry his own provisions. The weak and the poor were excused, but the wealthy who sought permission were not. Ka'b, a famous poet who had lost his court income on becoming Muslim, finally had the means to go, yet kept putting it off until it was too late. When the army returned and others offered false excuses, he chose to tell the truth, admitting he simply stayed back for his own interests. He stresses that honesty is not optional, that the hypocrites were never exposed or punished in this life, and that belonging to the Prophet's community brings more accountability. He then narrates the fifty-day boycott, the Prophet looking away, the earth closing in, the Ghassanid king's offer that Ka'b burned, and the joy of forgiveness. The lesson is that At-Tawbah calls for repentance from self-interest when the ummah needs us, that a place near the Prophet must be earned, and that the only refuge from Allah is Allah.

outline.heading: At-Tawbah and the 'hour of difficulty'
outline.gist: He picks a story meant to shape the approach to Ramadan; the Quran names the expedition the hour of difficulty, and Ka'b's own long narration is worth reading in full.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet named Tabuk openly
outline.gist: Unlike other campaigns he named the destination, marching north to meet Roman-allied Arab forces outside Arab lands rather than wait for them to come to Madinah.

outline.heading: No blame on the weak, the ill and the poor
outline.gist: It was August at date harvest, people were poor, and the journey demanded camels, shoes and food; those without means were excused.

outline.heading: Everyone carries his own weight
outline.gist: No one could go expecting others to feed him; those who could not afford it left in tears, and the story is about not staying back out of self-interest.

outline.heading: The rich who asked to stay behind
outline.gist: The blame falls on the wealthy who sought permission; with no roll call, staying back went unnoticed unless revelation exposed it.

outline.heading: Ka'b: never wealthier than then
outline.gist: Ka'b begins by saying he had never been better off than at the time of Tabuk.

outline.heading: Ka'b the poet of the Prophet
outline.gist: An early Ansari Muslim and celebrated poet, he was one of the Prophet's three poets who answered Quraysh's propaganda.

outline.heading: Poetry as the news and record of its age
outline.gist: Poems documented battles and spread news across Arabia, which is why early seerah books are full of poetry.

outline.heading: Why a famous poet had little money
outline.gist: Islam cut him off from the patronage of kings, leaving him dependent on selling his dates at the end of August.

outline.heading: 'Tomorrow I'll prepare': putting it off
outline.gist: He had two camels, the ideal case, but kept delaying each day until the army was too far ahead to catch.

outline.heading: Left among the excused and the hypocrites
outline.gist: Walking through Madinah he saw only the genuinely excused and known hypocrites, and himself among them.

outline.heading: A companion defends his absent brother
outline.gist: When someone mocked Ka'b on the road, a companion defended him; we owe our brothers good assumptions without needing reasons.

outline.heading: The Prophet receives the excuses
outline.gist: Returning after fifty days, he sat in the masjid and accepted people's excuses without demanding proof, praying for them even though most were lying.

outline.heading: Ka'b's turn and the displeased smile
outline.gist: Ka'b resolved to be truthful; the Prophet smiled at him in a way that showed displeasure and asked about his camels.

outline.heading: 'I have no excuse'
outline.gist: A master of words, he refused to talk his way out, fearing Allah would expose a lie, and admitted he stayed back for his own interest.

outline.heading: The surah of repentance from self-interest
outline.gist: We all need to repent from being preoccupied with our own lives when the ummah needs our commitment.

outline.heading: Honesty is not optional
outline.gist: Truthfulness earns no extra points; it is required. The Prophet said Ka'b had told the truth and sent him to await Allah's decision.

outline.heading: The liars were never exposed
outline.gist: Hypocrites were never called out or punished in this life; their oaths are for show, and Allah is not pleased with them.

outline.heading: Belonging to the ummah carries a price
outline.gist: Those who truly belong are tested and held to account more, and being counted among the Prophet's people is worth that price.

outline.heading: Pressure to recant, and seventy prayers for forgiveness
outline.gist: His clan urged him to make up an excuse; the Prophet prayed for the liars, yet Allah said even seventy prayers would not forgive them.

outline.heading: Two companions of Badr in the same position
outline.gist: Two righteous men had done the same, which steadied him; he explains he had attended every battle and valued the pledge of Aqabah above Badr.

outline.heading: The boycott and the Prophet looking away
outline.gist: No one was to speak to the three for fifty days; what hurt Ka'b most was the Prophet glancing at him in prayer and looking away.

outline.heading: The earth closes in
outline.gist: Even his beloved cousin would not answer whether Ka'b loved Allah and His Messenger, and the vast earth felt narrow.

outline.heading: Separated from their wives
outline.gist: On the fortieth day they were told to keep away from their wives, adding to their grief.

outline.heading: The Ghassanid king's offer
outline.gist: A letter invited him to the king's court with honour; recognising it as a test, he burned it rather than abandon the Prophet.

outline.heading: The good news and the best day of his life
outline.gist: On the fiftieth day the news of forgiveness came; Talhah embraced him and the Prophet, face shining, called it the best day since he was born.

outline.heading: Allah turned to the Prophet and those who followed him
outline.gist: Allah accepted the repentance of all who followed in the hour of difficulty, even those whose hearts nearly wavered.

outline.heading: The three who were held back, and earning your place
outline.gist: 'Left behind' means made to wait for judgment, setting the truthful apart from the liars; a place in the Prophet's nation must be earned.

outline.heading: Sitting under the Prophet's garment
outline.gist: Ka'b sitting under the Prophet's cloak symbolises where we hope to be, a place that has to be earned.

outline.heading: The ummah still needs you
outline.gist: The Prophet is not physically here but the story is the same: we cannot put self-interest before the work he left us.

outline.heading: No refuge from Allah except in Him; be with the truthful
outline.gist: They realised the only escape from Allah is to Him; after the command to be with the truthful, Ka'b never lied again.

outline.heading: Outro
