Jy6D9VP0myA.title: The Intention Behind Ramadan
Jy6D9VP0myA.one_line: Before planning Ramadan, set the intention: let it be the turning point that makes you someone who changes the ummah's course.
Jy6D9VP0myA.summary: A pre-Ramadan khutbah delivered while Gaza is being systematically starved. He opens with Ramadan as the month in which Allah calls hearts back, citing the narration of the month of barakah and the Prophet's three 'ameens' on the minbar, including the one against whoever lives through Ramadan without being forgiven. He then turns to Gaza and to three historical catastrophes: the Qarmatian massacre in Makkah and theft of the Black Stone, the Crusader capture of Jerusalem, and the Mongol sack of Baghdad. Each was reversed a generation or two later, often in Ramadan, once a new generation grew up refusing to accept the situation. His point is that this is not the worst the ummah has seen, so people should stop speculating about the end of time and ask what they are building for the next forty years. Responding to people who asked him to be more optimistic, he says his job is to sound an alarm, not a gentle reminder. Everyone will be asked what they did about what they witnessed. In the second khutbah he makes intention the first step of any Ramadan plan: decide why this Ramadan must change you. He ends by criticizing the community's fading advocacy and asks people to renew it as part of their Ramadan intention.

outline.heading: Opening
Nothing unites us like Ramadan
outline.gist: The fasting verse will open khutbahs all over the world for the coming weeks. Nothing unites the ummah like Ramadan, with Hajj a near second: a yearly chance to set things right and draw closer to Allah.

outline.heading: The King of hearts calls His servants
outline.gist: Anyone who works in a masjid in Ramadan sees faces never seen before filling it all month. That is not the masjid's doing: the King of hearts calls the hearts of His servants and they come.

outline.heading: A month of barakah
outline.gist: Ramadan has come to you, a month of barakah in which Allah covers you with mercy, forgives sins and answers dua, so show Him the best of yourselves; the wretched one is deprived of Allah's mercy in it. Then the Prophet climbed the three steps of the minbar saying ameen at each.

outline.heading: Three ameens: humiliated is the one not forgiven
outline.gist: Jibril made three duas; one was against whoever lives through Ramadan without being forgiven: may his nose be rubbed in the dust. You would have to work hard not to be forgiven in Ramadan.

outline.heading: Gaza is being starved
outline.gist: People in one of the richest regions on earth are being systematically starved after being ethnically cleansed, gunned down as they approach food trucks for their children, while the politicians we voted in support it. They will be shut out of the community until they admit the atrocities they backed.

outline.heading: The Qarmatians and the Black Stone
outline.gist: How bad can it get? In 317 AH the leader of an oppressive regime in eastern Arabia raided Makkah during Hajj, killed pilgrims in their thousands until the precinct of the Kaaba ran with blood, damaged the Kaaba and stole the Black Stone, holding it for 22 years before Muslims recovered it.

outline.heading: The Crusaders in Jerusalem
outline.gist: The Crusaders took the Holy Land, murdering Muslims and Jews, burning the masjid and turning it into a stable, and held it and parts of Lebanon, Jordan and Syria for decades until 583, in Ramadan, when it was retaken and Christians, Jews and Muslims could pray there again.

outline.heading: The Mongols in Baghdad
outline.gist: Less than a century later the Mongols burned Baghdad, killed everyone and threw the books of the greatest library on earth into the rivers until they ran red with blood and blue with ink. A couple of decades later, in 658 and again in Ramadan, they were driven back.

outline.heading: This is not the worst we have seen
outline.gist: We have always rebounded. This is not the end of time, not even close; your job is not to worry about when it comes but to know where you stand on your ummah's historical curve and what it needs from you. What were Hajj and Ramadan like in 318?

outline.heading: Every era thought it was Armageddon
outline.gist: Scholars of those eras wrote that the end was near, and it did not come in 583, 658, 1123, 1348 or today. The ummah is still large and full of people who care; despite his pessimism, it has rebounded from far worse.

outline.heading: A generation later, Ramadan was the spark
outline.gist: Most of these reversals came in Ramadan, a generation or two later, because the generation that suffered the catastrophe did not care enough; the next one grew up, refused to accept it and turned things around, as the Prophet gave a voice to the oppressed.

outline.heading: One spark from London, Ontario
outline.gist: Not a call for violence, but for each person to believe they will have an impact on the ummah's future. Even in a small city most people have never heard of, one person, or a hundred, can be one of the sparks that changes its history.

outline.heading: Work on what you can control
outline.gist: Believe it and be willing to work for it. Do not waste time on what you cannot control; what we see now was set in motion generations ago by people who stopped caring. The question is what you can do so it does not continue or happen again.

outline.heading: Asked to be more optimistic
outline.gist: What the next forty years look like depends on how we live now. Three people in one week asked him to be more optimistic; he would not be doing what he does if he did not believe to his core that this ummah can turn things around.

outline.heading: An alarm, not a gentle reminder
outline.gist: But at this point on the curve he is not a soft wake-up tone; he is here to sound an alarm that raises your heart rate and leaves you upset with yourself, as he is. Change cannot be slow and gradual: it has to be immediate, radical and huge.

outline.heading: You will be asked about what you witnessed
outline.gist: He has no stake in whether people listen; he knows his path. You will be asked not only about salah, zakah and family but about what you witnessed as part of this ummah and how you responded. 'I did nothing' is exactly the problem.

outline.heading: Aim higher: restore the truth
outline.gist: Where is the effect of witnessing tyranny and persecution on your life? Aim beyond Gaza and Palestine, for the ummah and for Allah, who created all this with truth: as long as falsehood prevails things will fail, and your job is to restore the truth and live it.

outline.heading: Every real tawbah story happens in Ramadan
outline.gist: He knows of no real story of repentance outside Ramadan: the decision that enough is enough, no longer a bystander focused on small things, happens in it, which is why those battles were won in it too.

outline.heading: Interlude
Intention first: why will you fast?
outline.gist: Number one in any Ramadan plan is intention: why you fast, pray and take part, beyond the ritual of hunger by day and late nights. Intend to come out a different person; doing better is no longer optional.

outline.heading: We were late, and children are starving
outline.gist: Because we were late, because he was late in figuring out his own life and impact, children carrying our names are starving to death. When Islam prevails it brings good to everyone, which is why we have an ethical obligation to live it and work for its success.

outline.heading: Your piece of the puzzle
outline.gist: Even if you spend your life strengthening a small community in a corner called London, Ontario, that is your piece of the puzzle: invisible from afar, but the One you do it for sees it and records it. The person no one notices may receive the greatest reward.

outline.heading: Spend the week on your why
outline.gist: They did the best they could within their limits in serving Allah, their deen and their nation. Spend the coming week asking why this Ramadan should be your turning point, find the reason that makes sense to you, and plan around it so that what is happening in Gaza never happens again.

outline.heading: Advocacy has faded: bring it back
outline.gist: He is disappointed at how the community has settled down since October and November: drag a crisis out six or seven weeks and people lose interest, though the killing and systematic starvation have not slowed. Those who were enthusiastic should bring it back as part of their Ramadan intention.

outline.heading: Outro
